pos: n. (first Lutheran bishop of Skalholt, c. 1512–1548; the young Icelander who began the Reformation in his own island)
etymology: From Old Norse Gizurr, a personal name; the patronymic Einarsson, son of Einar.
biblical_def: Gissur Einarsson was under thirty when he was made the first evangelical bishop of Iceland. Educated in Hamburg and at Wittenberg, he came home a convinced Lutheran, served as the old Catholic bishop's own secretary without revealing how far he had travelled, and on that bishop's death in 1540 was elected and then confirmed by the Danish king for the see of Skalholt. He proceeded carefully, almost quietly: he translated portions of Scripture, pressed the clergy to preach, worked the new church ordinance into Icelandic conditions a little at a time, and avoided the direct collision with the northern see at Holar that would have ruined him. He died at thirty-six, having held the office eight years. The dictionary records him because the Reformation in Iceland began in the hands of a man whose chief disadvantages were his youth and his gentleness, and because Paul anticipated the first of them exactly: “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers” (1Ti 4:12). The answer to being young in office is not to act older but to be exemplary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines youth as the part of life that succeeds to childhood, and a young person; an example as a pattern, a copy, that which is proposed to be imitated; and increase as augmentation, growth, that which is added.
webster_full: YOUTH, n. The part of life that succeeds to childhood; a young person; a young man.
EXAMPLE, n. [L. exemplum.] A pattern; a copy; a mode; that which is proposed to be imitated.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; also, produce, as of the earth; that which is added.
PLANT, v.t. [L. planto.] To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set, as a tree; to engraft, as principles.
scriptures: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Jer 1:6
Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
Jer 1:7
But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: The young Wittenberg-trained Icelander who became first Lutheran bishop of Skalholt in 1540 and died at thirty-six.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer error is the assumption that a reformation must be loud to be real, and the opposite assumption that caution is always cowardice. Gissur was cautious and he was also effective; his successor inherited a diocese that had already changed its preaching. He is equally a warning, since his reticence left the northern diocese untouched and the collision only postponed.

The principle to recover is that God answers the objection of youth by His commission rather than by waiting. Jeremiah raised exactly the plea, “Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child” (Jer 1:6), and the Lord refused it, saying “Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee” (Jer 1:7). Paul keeps the credit for growth with God and not with the workman, however gifted: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).

pos: n. (bishop of Skalholt, c. 1500–1576; published the first Icelandic handbook of worship and hymn collection)
etymology: From Old Norse Marteinn, Latin Martinus; the patronymic Einarsson, son of Einar.
biblical_def: Marteinn Einarsson succeeded Gissur Einarsson at Skalholt in 1549 and held the see until he resigned in 1556. He had spent years in England, which made him unusual among Icelandic churchmen, and he brought back a conviction that the people must be able to join in the service. His lasting work is a small one with large consequences: the first Icelandic handbook of worship, with a collection of hymns, printed in 1555, which gave Icelandic congregations forms of prayer and praise they could follow and answer. He was carried off to Denmark once by Jon Arason's sons in the northern rising and lived to see the island settled. The dictionary records him because the test he applied is the apostle's own, and it is a test of intelligibility: a man in the congregation must be able to say Amen. Paul asks how he can, “seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?” (1Co 14:16), and the question has only one honest answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amen as verily, so be it, used at the end of prayers; a liturgy as a formulary of public devotions; and distinctly as clearly, plainly, so as to be well understood.
webster_full: AMEN, adv. [Heb.] Verily; truly; certainly; so be it; used at the end of prayers to express assent to what has been said.
LITURGY, n. [Gr.] A formulary of public devotions; all the prescribed forms of public prayer in a church.
DISTINCTLY, adv. Clearly; plainly; without confusion; so as to be well understood.
HANDBOOK, n. A book of directions or instruction, of a size convenient to be held in the hand.
scriptures: Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Psa 47:7
For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding.
Rom 15:6
That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Skalholt's second evangelical bishop, who printed the first Icelandic handbook of worship and hymns in 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the treatment of public worship as a performance conducted in front of the congregation rather than by it. Latin did this by language; it can be done equally well in English by a form of service nobody has been taught, or by music nobody can sing. The congregation that cannot answer is in the position Paul describes, present but unable to assent, and the fault lies with those who lead.

The principle to recover is that the people's understanding is the measure of public worship. Ezra's Levites set the standard when the law was read: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). The psalm requires the mind to be engaged in the praise, “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7). And Paul names the end of it as a single voice, “That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God” (Rom 15:6), which cannot happen where only one mouth knows the words.

pos: n. (first Lutheran bishop of Holar, c. 1500–1569; under whom the first book was printed in Iceland)
etymology: From Old Norse Óláfr, ancestor's relic; the patronymic Hjaltason, son of Hjalti.
biblical_def: Olafur Hjaltason was given the hardest appointment in the Icelandic church. When Jon Arason, the last Catholic bishop of Holar, was beheaded in 1550, the northern diocese was left hostile, leaderless and convinced it had been wronged; Olafur was consecrated to it in 1552 and spent seventeen years making an unwilling territory evangelical. His most consequential act was to establish a printing press at Breidabolstadur under the Swedish printer Jon Matthiasson, which in 1562 produced his own handbook of worship, the first book printed on Icelandic soil. The press afterwards passed to Holar and printed the Icelandic Bible. The dictionary records him because a press in a remote diocese is a public act of confidence in the written word, and Scripture repeatedly commands the writing before it promises the spreading. The order is given to Habakkuk in a sentence: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). Plainness first, then running.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; to print as to take an impression of letters or figures; and a table as a flat surface, and a tablet on which anything is written or engraved.
webster_full: PRESS, n. A machine for printing; also, the art or business of printing and publishing.
PRINT, v.t. To take or receive an impression of letters or figures; to mark by pressing one thing on another.
TABLE, n. [L. tabula.] A flat surface; a thin flat piece of board or metal on which anything is written, engraved or painted.
ROLL, n. A writing or writings made into a cylindrical form; a volume; a scroll.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Jer 36:2

Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day.
Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.
Isa 30:8
Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever:
corruption_summary: First evangelical bishop of Holar, consecrated 1552 after Jon Arason's execution; set up the first printing press in Iceland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the preference for the immediate and spoken over the written and permanent, on the ground that print is cold. A sermon reaches the people in the room; a printed handbook reached every parish in a diocese that could not be visited twice in a decade, and it could be checked against Scripture at leisure by men who had no bishop to ask.

The principle to recover is that God has committed His word to writing on purpose, and that the writing survives its enemies. Jeremiah was told to take a roll and write all the words spoken to him, “Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee” (Jer 36:2); the king burned it, and the command came again, “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll” (Jer 36:28). Isaiah is given the reason for the labour: “note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8).

pos: n. (Icelandic Bible translator, c. 1514–1556; rendered the New Testament into Icelandic, printed 1540)
etymology: From Old Norse Oddr, a point or spear-point; the patronymic Gottskálksson, son of Gottskalk.
biblical_def: Oddur Gottskalksson gave Iceland the first book ever printed in its language, and it was the New Testament. The son of a Norwegian bishop of Holar, educated in Norway, Denmark and Germany, he came home to serve as secretary to the Catholic bishop of Skalholt and, by the account that has come down, did his translating in secret in a cowshed on the cathedral farm, because the work would have cost him his place and possibly his life. He went to Denmark to see it through the press and it appeared at Roskilde in 1540, translated from Luther's German with the Latin and Greek at hand. He drowned crossing a river in 1556. The dictionary records him because the Icelandic language was preserved as a written tongue largely by the Bible he began, and because the labour answers Christ's own account of what the Scriptures are for. They are not a monument to be guarded but a testimony to be read: “they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to translate as to interpret, to render into another language; inspiration as a supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind; and to testify as to bear witness, to affirm.
webster_full: TRANSLATE, v.t. [L. translatus.] To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men, ideas, notices or monitions by extraordinary or supernatural influence.
TESTIFY, v.i. [L. testificor.] To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to bear witness.
VERSION, n. [L. versio.] A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.
Rom 10:8
But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach;
corruption_summary: Translated the New Testament into Icelandic, by tradition in a cowshed; printed at Roskilde in 1540, the first Icelandic book.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the withholding of Scripture from the people in their own tongue, which Rome maintained by law for centuries and defended on the ground that an untrained reader would err. Men do err; and the remedy Scripture prescribes is teaching, not deprivation. The modern form of the same instinct substitutes the expert's summary for the text, so that a believer learns what the Bible is said to mean without ever having read what it says.

The principle to recover is that the word is meant to come near, into the mouth and the heart of the ordinary man. Moses said so of the law: “But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it” (Deu 30:14). Paul applies the same words to the gospel preached, “The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart” (Rom 10:8). And the whole of it is useful, not a part, since “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16).

“But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it” (Deu 30:14) — translated in secret while serving a Catholic bishop.

pos: n. (bishop of Holar, 1541–1627; printed the first complete Icelandic Bible in 1584 and held his see fifty-six years)
etymology: From Old Norse Guðbrandr, God's sword; the patronymic Thorlaksson, son of Thorlak.
biblical_def: Gudbrandur Thorlaksson held the see of Holar for fifty-six years and used them to put a Bible, a hymnbook and a catechism into every church in northern Iceland. Trained at Copenhagen in theology and mathematics, he took over the Holar press, cut his own woodcuts, and in 1584 produced the complete Icelandic Bible, five hundred copies, enough for every church in the island, paid for partly by a levy he obtained from the crown. He followed it with a hymnal in 1589, a book of sermons, and a graduale; he also drew the first tolerably accurate map of Iceland and calculated its latitude. The Bible he printed fixed the Icelandic language and is the reason Icelanders can still read their medieval sagas. The dictionary records him because he is the best European instance of what a long ministry and a press can do together. The word he printed outlasts everything he printed it on: “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the law as a rule of action prescribed by authority, and in Scripture the word of God; a testimony as a solemn declaration, and the divine revelation; and to wither as to fade, to lose freshness.
webster_full: LAW, n. A rule, particularly an established or permanent rule, prescribed by the supreme power of a state; in Scripture, the word of God, the revealed will of God.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact; in Scripture, the whole divine revelation.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
STATUTE, n. [L. statutum.] An act of the legislature of a state, commanding or prohibiting something; a positive law.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Psa 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Holar fifty-six years; his 1584 Icelandic Bible put a copy in every church and fixed the language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation attached to a work like his is the confusion of the vessel with the contents: a nation may come to revere the Bible that preserved its language as a monument of national culture while ceasing to read it as the word of God. Iceland has been near that, and so has every country with an old and beautiful version.

The principle to recover is the permanence of Scripture and its sufficiency for every use a soul has. The psalmist lists the offices one by one: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7), and again, “The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes” (Psa 19:8). Christ sets His own words above the frame of the world: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mat 24:35).

pos: n. (last Roman Catholic bishop of Holar, 1484–1550; resisted the Reformation in Iceland and was beheaded with two of his sons)
etymology: From Old Norse Jón, a form of John; the patronymic Árason, son of Ari.
biblical_def: Jon Arason was bishop of Holar for twenty-six years, a considerable Icelandic poet, and the last man to hold out against the Reformation north of the Alps with an army. He had sons, which his office forbade and his country overlooked, and when the Danish crown pressed the new ordinance on Iceland he treated it as a foreign imposition on an island that had governed its own church since the Commonwealth. In 1550 he and his sons took Skalholt by force and held the southern diocese. He was captured, and the Danish governor, fearing what a trial would produce, had him and two of his sons beheaded at Skalholt on 7 November 1550 without legal process. The dictionary honours the courage and the poetry, and names the errors plainly: his cause was Rome's, his method was the sword, and both were wrong. Christ forbade the second to Peter in the garden in terms that admit no exception for a bishop: “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sword as an offensive weapon worn at the side; carnal as fleshly, pertaining to flesh, not spiritual; and a stronghold as a fastness, a fort, a place of security.
webster_full: SWORD, n. An offensive weapon worn at the side, and used for thrusting or striking; the emblem of war and of authority.
CARNAL, adj. [L. carnalis.] Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to spiritual.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort or fortress; a place of security.
REVENGER, n. One who revenges; one who inflicts punishment for an injury or crime.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: Holar's last Catholic bishop, a poet who took Skalholt by arms and was beheaded with two sons in 1550 without trial.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet in this story and the dictionary names both. The first is Jon's own: the defence of the Roman system by force of arms, which assumes the church may wield the civil sword in its own cause. The second is the crown's: an execution without trial, which is murder whatever the victim's politics, and which gave the Icelandic Reformation a martyrdom it did not need and has never entirely lived down. A reformation advanced by an axe is advanced on the wrong principle.

The principle to recover is the distinction of the two swords and the spiritual character of the church's weapons. Christ grounded His own refusal of force in the nature of His kingdom: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36). Paul names the armoury the church actually has, for “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). The sword belongs to the magistrate alone, who “beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God” (Rom 13:4) — and a magistrate who kills without trial has abandoned the office that gave him the sword.

pos: n. (southern Icelandic episcopal see from 1056; the island's chief seat of learning and the place of Jon Arason's execution)
etymology: From Old Norse Skálholt, the wood by the hall; skáli, hall, and holt, a wood or rough ground.
biblical_def: Skalholt was the seat of the southern Icelandic bishopric from 1056 and for seven centuries the intellectual capital of the island. Its cathedral school taught Latin, theology and the law; its bishops kept the manuscripts; the medieval histories and law codes of Iceland were largely written, copied or preserved there. The Reformation came to it in 1540 with Gissur Einarsson, and ten years later Jon Arason was beheaded in its yard. The school continued until the see was moved to Reykjavik in 1785 after an earthquake, and the place is now a parish with a modern church and a small college. The dictionary records Skalholt because it is the clearest northern case of a church that was also a school for seven hundred years, and because that combination is required rather than optional. The priest is to be a man with knowledge to hand out: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knowledge as a clear and certain perception of that which exists; a school as a place in which persons are instructed; and to divide rightly as to handle or distribute with exactness.
webster_full: KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact; the perception of connection and agreement, or disagreement and repugnance of our ideas.
SCHOOL, n. [L. schola.] A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages, or any species of learning.
DIVIDE, v.t. [L. divido.] To part or separate; to deal out; to distribute in just proportion.
MESSENGER, n. One who bears a message or an errand; the bearer of a dispatch; one sent to communicate information.
scriptures: Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Ezr 7:10
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
corruption_summary: Iceland's southern see and chief school for seven centuries; reformed in 1540, and the site of Jon Arason's beheading in 1550.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the separation of piety from learning, which produces a ministry that is warm and uninstructed and a scholarship that is exact and unbelieving. Both halves are visible in the modern church. Skalholt held them together under conditions of real hardship, teaching Latin and theology on a volcanic island at the edge of the inhabited world, and the result was a literate clergy and a literate people.

The principle to recover is that the destruction of a people follows the failure of its teachers. Hosea traces the ruin to its source without softening it: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee” (Hos 4:6). Paul requires labour of the workman, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). And Ezra is the pattern, a man who “had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezr 7:10) — seeking, doing, and teaching, in that order.

pos: n. (northern Icelandic episcopal see from 1106; site of the press that printed the Icelandic Bible)
etymology: From Old Norse Hólar, the hills or hillocks; plural of hóll, a hill.
biblical_def: Holar was the northern Icelandic bishopric, founded in 1106, and for four hundred years the rival and complement of Skalholt. Its cathedral school trained the clergy of the north; Jon Arason was its last Roman bishop and died for the old religion; Olafur Hjaltason was its first evangelical one, and Gudbrandur Thorlaksson, who followed, made it the printing centre of the island. From a turf-and-timber settlement in a northern valley there came a complete vernacular Bible, a hymnal, a graduale and a book of sermons, in a language spoken by perhaps fifty thousand people at the edge of the habitable world. The see was abolished in 1801 and the place is now a church and an agricultural college. The dictionary records Holar because the reach of the printed word is not limited by the obscurity of the place it is printed in. The psalmist describes the carrying power of God's testimony in terms no press could improve: “Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world” (Psa 19:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a line as a measure, a cord, and figuratively a direction or extent; the Gentiles as the nations distinct from Israel; and salvation as the redemption of man from sin and liability to eternal death.
webster_full: LINE, n. [L. linea.] A measuring line or cord; extent; limit; also, a rule or direction.
GENTILE, n. [L. gentilis.] In the Scriptures, a pagan; a worshipper of false gods; any person not a Jew or a Christian.
SALVATION, n. The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death, and the conferring on him everlasting happiness.
UTTERMOST, adj. Extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree.
scriptures: Psa 19:4
Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun,
But I say, Have they not heard? Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.
For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.
Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
corruption_summary: Iceland's northern see from 1106 and the island's printing centre; the Icelandic Bible of 1584 came from its press.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the assumption that the important work of the church is done at its centres, so that a remote diocese is a place to be supplied rather than a place that supplies. Holar reverses the expectation. It printed the Bible that fixed a national language, and it did so after the great sees of Europe had been printing for a century.

The principle to recover is the intended universality of the word's spread and the smallness of the instruments God uses for it. Paul applies the psalm to the gospel's advance, that “their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Rom 10:18). The commission he quotes over himself is drawn from Isaiah and reaches further than any diocese: “I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth” (Act 13:47), and the prophet had said that raising up Jacob alone would have been “a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant” (Isa 49:6).

pos: n. (Icelandic pastor and poet, 1614–1674; author of the Hymns of the Passion, written as leprosy took him)
etymology: From Old Norse Hallgrímr, stone-helm; the patronymic Pétursson, son of Petur.
biblical_def: Hallgrimur Petursson is the greatest religious poet Iceland has produced and he wrote his best work out of a ruined life. Sent abroad as a boy, he was apprenticed to a smith in Copenhagen, rescued for schooling by Brynjolfur Sveinsson, and came home to a poor coastal parish; he married a woman who had been a captive of Barbary corsairs, lost a daughter, lost his house and books to fire, and contracted leprosy, which killed him. Between 1656 and 1659 he wrote the Passíusálmar, fifty Hymns of the Passion, a meditation on the sufferings of Christ which has been read aloud or broadcast in Iceland every Lent since, and the funeral hymn that is still sung at Icelandic graves. The dictionary records him because his subject and his circumstance explain each other. A man losing his body to a disease without remedy wrote on the one wound that heals: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the passion as the last sufferings of Christ; affliction as the state of being afflicted, calamity, distress; and a stripe as a blow with a lash or whip, and the wound so made.
webster_full: PASSION, n. [L. passio.] The last suffering of the Savior; the sufferings of Christ in the garden and on the cross.
AFFLICTION, n. [L. afflictio.] The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief; the cause of continued pain of body or mind.
STRIPE, n. A stroke made with a lash, whip or rod; also, the wound or hurt made by a lash.
TRANSGRESSION, n. [L. transgressio.] The violation of a law or command; the breach of a divine command; sin.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
corruption_summary: Iceland's greatest poet, a leprous parish pastor whose fifty Hymns of the Passion have been read every Lent since 1659.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern reluctance to dwell on the sufferings of Christ, which is defended as a preference for the resurrection and amounts in practice to a gospel without an atonement. Hallgrimur spent fifty hymns on the passion and did not find it morbid, because he knew what his own suffering was worth without it. The matching error treats his affliction as the source of his insight, as if sorrow itself taught him; it did not. The text did.

The principle to recover is that Christ's sufferings were substitutionary and that the believer's own are brief by comparison. Isaiah describes a Man no one wished to look at, “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” (Isa 53:3). Peter states the transaction and its purpose together: He “bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness” (1Pe 2:24). And Paul weighs a whole lifetime of trouble against what follows it, calling it “our light affliction, which is but for a moment” (2Co 4:17), set against an eternal weight of glory.

pos: n. (bishop of Skalholt, 1666–1720; author of the house postil read in Icelandic homes for a century and a half)
etymology: Latinised Icelandic Vídalín, from Víðidalur, the willow valley.
biblical_def: Jon Vidalin was the finest preacher Iceland produced and the one whose preaching actually reached the whole nation, because it was printed. Bishop of Skalholt from 1698 until his death, he published between 1718 and 1720 the Vídalínspostilla, a book of sermons on the Gospel readings for the church year, written in a hard, vivid, plain Icelandic that spared no one and gave no comfort cheaply. For a hundred and fifty years it was read aloud in Icelandic farmhouses on Sunday evenings, in districts where a minister came seldom and a church service was a day's ride off, and it shaped the religion of the island more than any pulpit could. The dictionary records him because the household reading of a printed sermon is a lawful and historically immense form of the ministry of the word, and because the apostle names house-to-house teaching alongside public preaching without ranking them: he taught “you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a postil as a marginal note, and a homily or exposition of the gospel; to exhort as to incite by words to good deeds; and instant as pressing, urgent, importunate.
webster_full: POSTIL, n. [L. post illa, after those words.] A marginal note; a short comment or exposition on a text of Scripture; a homily.
EXHORT, v.t. [L. exhortor.] To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge to any good conduct or to laudable deeds.
INSTANT, adj. [L. instans.] Pressing; urgent; importunate; earnest.
LONGSUFFERING, n. Continuance of patience under provocation or injury; patient endurance.
scriptures: And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Skalholt; his 1718 book of sermons was read aloud in Icelandic farmhouses on Sunday evenings for a century and a half.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the loss of family worship, and with it the loss of any Christian instruction that is not delivered by a professional in a building. Where the household no longer reads, prays and sings, the whole weight of a family's religion rests on an hour a week, and the hour cannot carry it. Iceland kept its faith through two centuries of poverty and isolation largely on an evening reading, and the book it read was a bishop's sermons.

The principle to recover is that the house is a place of instruction by divine appointment, and that the head of it is charged with the teaching. Moses makes the occasions continuous: “And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 11:19). Paul charges Timothy to preach without regard to convenience, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). And the psalmist's resolution begins where a man's rule actually reaches: “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2).
